picks.style: late antique consolation lament, bowed viol and small harp, grave low male voice, slow, elegiac, sparse
picks.why: The book's opening cry — 'My days are numbered not by time but Grief' — the most famous lament in the work and complete in itself.

picks.style: orphic ballad, solo lyre and low drone, keening tenor, unhurried, spellbinding, building to a break
picks.why: The Orpheus meter, ending on 'Love hath no law but her own will' and the fatal backward look.

picks.style: cosmic hymn, chamber organ and viols, layered choir over a held drone, measured, luminous, processional
picks.why: 'This mutual love courses eternal makes' — the concord of the elements laid out season by season, pure refrain material.

picks.style: roman satiric declamation, plucked lyre and hand drum, sardonic biting male voice, brisk, driving, insolent
picks.why: 'Must I be always only a listener? Never strike back' — the line that opens satire as a genre, and it opens itself.

picks.style: urban street rant, low strings and clattering percussion, hoarse restless male voice, hurried, jostling, claustrophobic
picks.why: Rome by night — carts, curses, elbows — landing on 'Only with great wealth can one sleep in the city.'

picks.style: grave latin moral chant, cello drone and struck bronze, stern baritone, slow, admonitory, gathering weight
picks.why: The tower image from Satire X: the higher the wish, the vaster the fall — the passage the whole vanity-of-wishes tradition rests on.

picks.style: gothic elegy, sustained strings and distant bell, cold clear soprano, slow, desolate, echoing
picks.why: The nun's despair told through what she hears — the midnight bell, the hollow gale, the hoarse resounding flood.

picks.style: graveyard-school elegy, harpsichord and viola da gamba, plaintive tenor, unhurried, solemn, sea-wind atmosphere
picks.why: Ruined abbey above the sea with a fourfold 'Far other' refrain already built into the stanza.

picks.style: sentimental english air, guitar and flute, tender mezzo, gentle, grieving, strophic
picks.why: The lament over the dead turtle-dove — 'How silent is the voice... How still, how frozen is the constant heart'.

picks.style: georgian pleasure-garden song, harpsichord and violin, arch witty soprano, brisk, dancing, teasing
picks.why: Written as a song for Ranelagh, with the cocked hat and the masculine air — the one candidate built to be sung.

picks.style: english pastoral ode, recorder and lute, warm tenor, lilting, springlike, unhurried
picks.why: 'When Spring gives up the reins of Time to Summer's glowing hand' — clean singable six-line stanzas and a real image.

picks.style: ruins ode, low strings and chamber organ, declamatory baritone, slow, questioning, hollow
picks.why: An ubi sunt over the Roman campagna — 'Where are the bold, the busy throngs' — repeated question as refrain.

picks.style: border ghost ballad, fiddle and bodhrán, stark unaccompanied opening female voice, slow, uncanny, strophic
picks.why: 'In glided Margaret's grimly ghost, and stood at William's feet' — the most famous ballad opening in the book.

picks.style: accusing ballad, plucked harp and drone, wounded female voice, insistent, rising, strophic
picks.why: The ghost's reproach is a hammering chain of 'Why did you' questions — refrain-shaped already.

picks.style: english pastoral ballad, acoustic guitar and whistle, warm clear female vocal, moderate, tender, storytelling
picks.why: Edwin and Emma's opening — cottage, sheltering wood, and a mother whose only wish is to see her blest and die.

picks.style: georgian drawing-room air, harpsichord and cello, light amused soprano, moderate, elegant, ending on a wink
picks.why: The moral of the sea-bathing poem, closing on 'Plunge — and a new-born Venus rise'.

picks.style: comic english art song, plucked strings and bassoon, dry playful tenor, bouncing, mock-learned
picks.why: Venus out of the sea-froth used to tease a lady into the water — a complete conceit in one turn.

picks.style: theatrical patter song, fortepiano and pit strings, bold brassy female voice, quick, defiant, comic
picks.why: Constance after the play — 'a bustling woman lives thro' every storm... I had no weapon left me but my tongue'.

picks.style: revolutionary industrial anthem, anvil percussion and low brass, massed male chorus, marching, iron, rousing
picks.why: Factory whistles as a morning hymn to unity, then the 'Comrade, comrade, have no fear' refrain arrives.

picks.style: workers' chorus, hammered percussion and accordion, layered voices, steady driving pulse, defiant, building
picks.why: The refrain doubles and closes — 'You're a new link forged in here — have no fear!'

picks.style: shaiva devotional chant, tanpura drone and small bell, deep male voice, very slow, reverent, sparse
picks.why: Only candidate, but a real closing benediction: meditate on this and Śiva-hood enters your own heart.
